title: Neural Renormalization Group Flow for Percolation
authors: Anaclara Alvez, Luca Camagna, Sergio Chibbaro, Cyril Furtlehner, François Landes, Gianluca Manzan, Lorenzo Mensi
abstract: Machine learning offers a possible route to data-driven real-space renormalization when the relevant observables are nonlocal and difficult to prescribe explicitly. We explore this idea for two-dimensional site percolation developping a supervised, scale-shared neural architecture. The model recursively applies the same learned coarse-graining rule across scales, producing a latent field from which the crossing probability is predicted, while a corresponding fine-graining decoder reconstructs the largest-cluster mask. Trained only on small lattices, the model extrapolates to substantially larger systems, recovers the spanning cluster with high fidelity, and produces observables obeying the expected finite-size scaling near the critical point. We observe that to get such performance it is key that the learned latent representation exhibits critical fluctuations and scale-dependent flows consistent with the renormalization-group structure of percolation.
summary: This paper proposes using a scale-shared neural network architecture to perform real-space renormalization group calculations for 2D site percolation. By forcing the network to learn scale-dependent transformations, the model accurately predicts critical observables and exhibits finite-size scaling behavior, demonstrating the power of integrating physical symmetries into machine learning models.
main_problem: Developing a data-driven, real-space renormalization group (RG) approach using machine learning to handle nonlocal observables in scale-invariant systems.
main_result: The model successfully predicts critical percolation observables, showing that the learned latent representation must exhibit critical fluctuations consistent with RG theory to achieve accurate finite-size scaling.
method: A novel, scale-shared encoder-decoder neural architecture is trained to recursively apply coarse-graining and fine-graining rules across multiple scales.
model_or_system: The study analyzes two-dimensional site percolation on a square lattice, a classic model for studying critical phenomena and phase transitions.
key_observables:
Percolation probability ($\Pi$), order parameter ($P_\infty$), and the finite-size scaling variable $x = (p - p_c)L^{1/
u}$.
important_parameters:
The critical probability $p_c$ and the correlation length exponent $
u$ are key parameters tested against theoretical predictions.
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that the RG structure provides a necessary inductive bias that allows the network to extrapolate accurately to much larger systems than those used for training.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the model's prediction of the spanning cluster mask at large sizes, the collapse of predicted observables onto finite-size scaling functions, and the schematic of the scale-shared RG-inspired architecture.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of data-driven RG for nonlocal observables, details the scale-shared encoder-decoder architecture (encoder for coarse-graining, decoder for reconstruction), trains the model using specific losses, and validates its performance by demonstrating adherence to known finite-size scaling laws.
why_interesting: The explicit incorporation of RG principles into a neural network architecture provides a powerful, data-driven tool for analyzing critical phenomena, which shares conceptual links with how quantum critical points are studied in many-body physics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Site-percolation configuration at criticality (left), mask of the spanning cluster (center), and prediction of the neural network (right). The lattice size is L = 1024, which lies outside the training range and therefore probes finite-size extrapolation.

FIG. 2. Scale-shared RG-inspired encoder-decoder architec- ture. The encoder applies the same learned coarse-graining map fθ at every scale until the lattice is represented by a single latent vector, from which a readout gθ predicts the percola- tion probability. The decoder applies the same learned fine- graining map f ′ θ at every scale, combining coarse information with encoder features to reconstruct the largest-cluster mask.

FIG. 3. Finite-size scaling of the learned percolation observ- ables. Top Panel: predicted crossing probability bΠ(p, L) as a function of p, with inset showing the collapse as a function of x = (p −pc)L1/ν. Bottom Panel: predicted order parameter ˆP∞(p, L) obtained from the decoder output, compared with the target cluster mass fraction. The inset shows the behavior above the critical point and the corresponding estimate of β.

FIG. 4. Classification and reconstruction performance as a function of the rescaled occupation probability x = (p − pc)L1/ν. Top: encoder accuracy for the percolation label. Bottom: decoder accuracy for the largest-cluster mask. The largest size used during training is L = 64, while the test sizes extend up to L = 1024. For each value of x, the reported value is the median over N = 5000 test samples. Error bars indi- cate bootstrap uncertainty over test samples. Insets show the performance at criticality as a function of L.

FIG. 5. Top:Projection of the coarsest latent representation Φ onto principal components computed from critical samples at the largest training size. Points show critical samples. Colors correspond to distinct connectivity patterns, including non- percolating configurations (light blue), configurations span- ning in both directions (orange), and other percolating pat- terns related by rotations (green). Six clusters are clearly apparent. Arrows indicate the motion of the distribution Φ(p, L)’s centroid as the lattice size increases, for values of p below and above pc, providing an empirical visualization of the learned scale flow.
